catalog_quote: In most languages stress, a slight raise of the pitch, is not relevant. Only PWG has a system that is meaningful even for grammar. The following presentation refers to Inor, where these phenomena were investigated in detail. The basic stress rule is: a final closed syllable is stressed; when the final syllable is open, the stress is penultimate: ä-säp'ärä 'he broke_rel.', yəsäβ'ər 'he breaks'. Final -e, -i are always stressed: yəsäwər-'i 'one breaks/they break it_m.' (a synchronic interpretation of these as */äy/ and */əy/ does not work for other reasons). Long vowels and diphthongs behave like a sequence of two vowels: bi'id 'house', ga'ara 'loin'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (a slight pitch rise) falls on a word-final closed syllable; if the final syllable is open, stress is penultimate. Final -e and -i are always stressed regardless. Long vowels and diphthongs count as two syllables (so a long vowel/diphthong gets stress on its second mora when final). Overlaid on this: the historical loss of the multifunctional suffix -m after final short vowels left a functionally distinctive final stress (main-clause säpär'ä 'he broke' vs. subordinate -säp'ärä), an 'accentual harmony' rule that also stresses a short-vowel open penult before a stressed final syllable (other than -e/-i), giving two stress peaks, and some suffixes (e.g. definite future -k'we) that carry their own stress without altering the host's.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No 'secondary stress' as such; the source describes sequences of two full stresses ('accentual harmony': säp'ä'rä 'he broke', 'with the acoustic effect of a sequence of two high tones, with two peaks') and 'dual stress' from self-stressed suffixes (yəsäβ'ər-k'w'e 'he will break').
new_statements.exceptions: Final -e/-i always stressed; grammatically distinctive final stress replacing lost -m (main vs. subordinate verb forms; also in -CC'e/i-'i sequences, säpärš'i'i 'you(sg.f.) broke it'); accentual-harmony double stress; suffixes with inherent stress. Leslau 1992 (snippet only) gives a different rule for Ennemor/Endegen/Gyeto: stress final in verbs, penultimate in nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (verb and noun forms cited in isolation; described as 'a slight raise of the pitch'). Statement is given for Peripheral Western Gurage with Inor as the representative variety, resting on Hetzron 1970's detailed Ennemor (= Inor) study.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement is for Inor (= Ennemor/Ennämor, Glottolog inor1238), named explicitly by Hetzron as the representative of Peripheral Western Gurage (PWG: Inor, Ener, Endegagn, Gyeto); his data derive from his 1970 Ennemor study. Wendimu 2011 (silent on stress) is based on Gunchire/Andahore speakers. Leslau's snippet rule covers 'Ennemor, Endegen and Gyeto' jointly.

sources.note: Second-hand survey: 'Hetzron (1970) discusses Inor stress and vowel length, and declares that closed final syllables or final -i and -e are stressed, otherwise the penult is stressed. In Chaha, it seems as if the penultimate syllable is favoured.' Concludes Ethio-Semitic stress 'awaits a more thorough investigation'.
